headline: Default shared filesystem and broad write/network access create medium prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks; compliance risk is low absent a documented residency mismatch.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can read/write the host working directory and uses shared memory by default, while unstructured reads/writes documents in its container and processes files. If the pair shares files or copied outputs, attacker-controlled document content from B can be treated as instructions by A. The interaction is plausible in default orchestration, though not proven documented.
conditions: IF agent_a ingests files produced by agent_b without provenance checks
IF the two agents share a workspace or copied document channel
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Add provenance tags to all B outputs
Strip instructions from parsed documents before A reads them
Require human review before A executes file-derived directives
requires-engineering: enforce content-type and trust boundaries in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and A explicitly handles API keys and developer-passed crew data. B processes documents, images, and text, so shared workspace access can expose sensitive inputs from A to B or vice versa. The blast radius is multiple work products or secrets, but the profiles do not show uncontrolled third-party upload by B.
conditions: IF agent_a stores secrets or crew data in the shared working directory
IF agent_b can read the same directory or mounted volume
mitigations: Use separate encrypted volumes
Keep secrets out of shared files
Mount B read-only on sanitized inputs
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
requires-engineering: add per-agent access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have filesystem write and subprocess execution, and A has broad network egress while B has allowlisted egress. Concurrent writes to the same directory or shared artifacts can overwrite each other or corrupt state. This is a default-pathway conflict because neither profile shows locking or isolation between the pair.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or artifact set
IF the orchestrator does not serialize writes or provide locks
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize write phases
Use file locks for shared artifacts
Disable concurrent subprocess writes to shared paths
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate crew outputs from broad tool use, and B processes documents and text that may be derived from A. If B treats A's output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream parsing or transformation. The profiles show no verification gate between them, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated text or documents as input
IF B does not independently verify extracted facts before acting
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B acts
Require source-document citations for A outputs
Compare A outputs against original files
Flag low-confidence fields for human review
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile, so a compliance breach is not established. A handles developer-passed crew data and secrets, while B processes documents and text, but the profiles do not show a specific regulated data class or cross-border policy conflict. I cite both because the risk depends on their combined data handling, though the evidence is weak.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is routed through both agents
IF their retention or residency policies differ in deployment
mitigations: Classify data before routing
Block regulated data from unapproved paths
Document retention settings for both agents
Review vendor privacy terms
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement and audit logging
